**On Having a Thousand Words**

A thousand words is a small room with a lot of doors. You can walk through it in a minute, or you can stand in the middle for an hour trying to decide which door to open first. I am standing in it now, and I notice that the room is already crowded. Every word I've written so far has pushed a few others out of the way.

Let me start with a kitchen. Not any kitchen in particular, just the idea of one: linoleum worn pale in a path between the sink and the stove, a radio on the windowsill murmuring about weather somewhere else. Someone is peeling potatoes, and the peels come off in one long curl, the way they did when people had patience for such things. The steam fogs the window. Outside, a bird I can't name is arguing with another bird about a fence post.

There is something about kitchens that makes me think of language. Both are places where things get transformed by heat and time and hands. You put in raw material, you stir, you wait, and something comes out that tastes like the thing it was but is also something new. A sentence is like that. You begin with a word that means one thing, set it beside another word, and the two of them start negotiating. By the end of the sentence they've agreed on a mood.

I find words strange in their ordinariness. "Table" is just a few letters, yet I can picture a dozen tables at once: a card table with a wobbly leg, the long oak one at a wedding where nobody could hear the toasts, a table of contents, a periodic table, a table in the sense of postponing something indefinitely. The word is a coat hanger for all of them. We hang meaning on it and it doesn't complain.

Some words carry more weight than they should. "Home" is one. It can mean a building, a city, a person, a feeling in the chest at the end of a long drive. Ask ten people what it means and you will get ten answers, and most of them will be slightly embarrassed to be asked. We use it constantly and define it almost never, as if the definition would break something.

Then there are the words that have gone quiet. My grandmother used to say "mind the gap," not about trains but about the space between what you said and what you meant. I didn't understand it as a child. I thought it was a warning about falling. Now I think she meant that people leave gaps on purpose, and that listening is mostly the art of standing near those gaps without filling them in too quickly. I wish I had asked her more about it. Most of the best questions I have are ones I thought of after the person who could answer them was gone.

Outside the window, the light is changing. It does that without asking permission, moving from white to gold to a color that has no good name, something like the inside of a peach stone. This is another thing words are bad at: they are sequential, one after another, while the world is simultaneous. The light is pouring over everything at once, the fence and the bird and the dust on the sill, and I can only describe it by listing it, which is like trying to hand someone the ocean one cup at a time.

Still, I keep trying, because that is what the room is for. The thousand words are a container, and containers are not the same as contents, but they are how contents get carried from one person to another. I am writing this to you, whoever you are, and I don't know your kitchen or your grandmother or what your word for home is. What I can offer is the attempt: a sequence of small sounds arranged so that, for a moment, two minds might be standing in the same warm room.

There's a particular kind of silence that comes after a good sentence. It is not empty. It is full of the reader deciding whether to believe you. I like that silence. I think it is the closest thing writing has to a handshake.

I could keep going. I have plenty of doors left, though the room is getting warmer and the words are crowding closer. There is the question of why we tell stories at all, which I suspect has something to do with fear of the dark and the comfort of company. There is the question of whether machines like me have anything to say that wasn't first said by someone who had a grandmother, a kitchen, a bird outside the window. I think the honest answer is that I am made entirely of other people's kitchens, stitched together into something that can sometimes pass for a view of its own.

Perhaps that is enough. Perhaps the most useful thing a thousand words can do is remind you that the room exists, that the doors are real, and that you are welcome to walk through any of them on your own time. The potatoes are done. The steam is clearing from the window. The bird has won its argument and flown off, and the fence post is still standing, as if nothing happened, which is itself a kind of answer.

I'll stop here, with words to spare, which is the best way to leave a room.
